items.title: Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: The only new person, new persons, was me and Cecil McBee. That’s his first time out.

ctx.x: I’ll say this, at one point my knees were shaking you know. You know when I decided to leave Howard University with my pharmacy studies and grapple with this thing, that was the moment where I said I know I can do this. And so anything that came after that was like gravy for me because I, you know, I knew I could play that trumpet now the way I was hearing it. And so what stood out for me was that Jackie McLean, so I was sent to Jackie McLean, who actually is the guy responsible for me being where I am in terms…

And he says, “Do you have any tunes?” I said, “Yes I do.” He says, “Let me hear them, let me play them.” He says, “Okay I’m putting you on my next record date.” Now I’ve told that story many times and every time people said you’ve got to be kidding. He hadn’t heard you yet. I said, “Well he was going on what Jim Harrison said, ‘Hey you know there’s a new trumpet player in town.’” You know. Boom. And so, and then to get on that, there was a place called Len Oliver’s Studio, it was a famous place on 89th and…
That’s a terrific story. I’m going to make a proposal here. We’ve been talking for an hour and I wonder if I could engage you for a part 2 in the near future?

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: He trained Bobby Hutcherson, Charles Tolliver, and let me see, and myself.

ctx.x: Well my question is, moving from placing quarter notes and swing and playing on top of the beat, this was a totally different task for you it seems like, playing a bass line repetitively in some cases basically the similar thing all the way through, while other players did their explorations. Like you were the anchor. And I wonder if you enjoyed that role, for sometimes the songs could go on for eight or nine minutes. How do you keep your concentration?

You don’t concentrate, you just feel it. Something like that, by that I mean it’s just a vibe. You are now as a bassist, you are now being rather responsible to maintain the bass line that would support all that is happening beyond you melodically, harmonically, etcetera, etcetera. It was something, quite frankly, that I was already sort of familiar with. Number one my second group — my first group that I performed with in New York City was with Jackie McLean. He trained Bobby Hutcherson, Charles Tolliver, and…
This is sort of a personal question, do you feel you are a spiritual man? Does faith play a significant role in your life?

items.title: Charles Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I wanted to read something that Cecil McBee said in a conversation I had with him last November.

ctx.x: Yes. I had a question that had to do with spirituality. And I think I’m guilty of for too long when people bring up spirituality I think of religion or faith. And I wanted to read something that Cecil McBee said in a conversation I had with him last November. And it was about spirituality and different periods in jazz. And he said, “well if it ain’t spiritual don’t play it. You know your spirit is what makes you play the instrument. If you’re not spiritual you ain’t feeling nothing. Elvin Jones used to say, ‘if…

Oh yeah. I basically want to have a spiritual connection to the musicians that I’m performing with at the time and so I have their capabilities in mind. Sometimes when I’m writing something I says well so-and-so-and-so would probably like to solo off this or play this you know. So there is that spiritual connection to your fellow musicians you know, a lot when you’re writing songs you know if you are looking for some sort of inspiration. And my inspiration generally is rhythmical, dealing with the drums you know.…
